sourceReferences.label: Torn Organized Crime 2.0
sourceReferences.notes: Used as structural inspiration for role-sensitive planning, branching action checkpoints, and outcome ladders.

questTypes.label: Gathering / Extraction
questTypes.notes: Locating a viable site, harvesting or extracting safely, and returning graded output.

questTypes.label: Escort
questTypes.notes: Protecting people or cargo through a route that may branch into ambush, pursuit, or recovery states.

questTypes.label: Extermination
questTypes.notes: Locating a threat source, breaching it, and confirming the threat has actually been removed.

questTypes.label: Porter
questTypes.notes: Load planning, endurance travel, checkpoint handling, and delivery integrity.

questTypes.label: Crafting
questTypes.notes: Workshop-stage production with quality and loss branches at the natural craft checkpoints.

questTypes.label: Menial Labor
questTypes.notes: Sustained work shifts where output, exhaustion, congestion, and small hazards matter more than combat.

questTypes.label: Masterwork Crafting
questTypes.notes: Longer expert commissions with repeated precision checks and catastrophic-loss states.

questTypes.label: Maritime Salvage
questTypes.notes: Waterborne recovery jobs where route, rigging, currents, and recovery timing govern the result.

checkKinds.notes: Flat stat gate or weighted stat contribution.
Rank-based check against an authored player skill.
Presence of a learned active ability unlocks a bonus path or mitigation.
Presence of a spell grants a bonus branch, safety net, or alternate route.
A required or optional tool/item key affects execution quality or safety.
Consumable or carried item input changes the branch result.
Equipment class or slot tag needed for the route.
Crew size can help or hurt depending on noise, congestion, load, or formation pressure.

records.name: Field Gathering and Extraction Contract
records.summary: A reusable template for herb, shell, ore, peat, and similar field collection jobs where locating the site and grading the haul matter as much as the harvest itself.

notes: Current authored data emphasizes observation, extraction, and field handling rather than a dedicated traversal skill.
The instantiated quest should narrow the final tool and method set to the actual extraction mode.

classification.usualFailureProfile: The crew most often loses quantity, quality, or an entire site window rather than dying outright, though local fauna or terrain can still injure workers.

roleSlots.label: Spotter
roleSlots.notes: Reads the ground, water, or shelf and picks the viable patch.

roleSlots.label: Extractor
roleSlots.notes: Cuts, pries, hauls, or gathers the material while preserving usable yield.

partySizeRules.effect: A solo gatherer can still finish, but yield and recovery options fall sharply if something spooks or collapses.
Too many hands trample sites, muddy water, and reduce the chance of finding the cleanest pocket.

outcomeMetrics.label: Yield
outcomeMetrics.description: How much usable material is brought back.

outcomeMetrics.label: Quality
outcomeMetrics.description: How refined, clean, or saleable the gathered lot remains.

outcomeMetrics.label: Safety
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the party avoids bites, falls, spoilage, and contamination.

outcomeMetrics.label: Timeliness
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the gathered lot returns before rot, weather, or market windows close.

failureStates.label: Empty Site
failureStates.description: The crew spends the window on a poor patch and returns with too little to satisfy the contract.

failureStates.label: Contaminated Lot
failureStates.description: Mud, rot, or poor sorting ruins the salable portion of the haul.

failureStates.label: Field Injury
failureStates.description: The run turns dangerous when a fall, beast, or current forces a retreat.

nodes.label: Read the ground
nodes.summary: Pick the patch, shelf, seam, or shoal worth working before the crew commits its time.

checks.notes: Spotting the viable patch before trampling it.
Separating surface signs from bad leads.
Improves the read on spoor, seams, and water clarity.
A second set of eyes helps, but too many boots ruin the site.
Fog, rain, or churned water can still obscure the site.

criticalSuccess.summary: The crew finds the richest pocket with minimal waste.

success.summary: The site looks workable and the team moves in.

failure.summary: A bad read spooks the site or drives the team into unstable ground.

criticalFailure.summary: The window is wasted on a dead patch and the contract collapses before extraction starts.

nodes.label: Careful extraction
nodes.summary: Cut, pry, gather, or dredge the goods while preserving usable quantity and quality.

checks.notes: Delicate cutting, lifting, and packing.
Actually getting the material free.
Baseline carrying capacity for the harvest.
Cleaner cuts preserve more sellable material.
Surface mineral or shell extraction speeds up with proper striking tools.
Loose shelves and hidden burrows can still turn the run.
A steady ward reduces cuts, slips, and glancing impacts during extraction.

criticalSuccess.summary: The crew works cleanly and fills the best containers first.

success.summary: Most of the haul comes free in good condition.

partial.summary: The team gets enough, but bruises or grit drag down part of the lot.

failure.summary: The extraction turns messy and the site pushes back.

nodes.label: Handle the disturbance
nodes.summary: A spooked beast, collapsing lip, or foul current forces a decision between recovery and retreat.

checks.notes: Avoiding the worst of the hazard.
Important if the site turns into a scramble, collapse, or rough recovery.
A defensive stance lets the crew disengage with more of the haul intact.
A steady ward is a cheap safety net against cuts, stings, and glancing blows.
Some sites simply turn bad after being disturbed.

success.summary: The crew breaks contact and keeps a salvageable lot.

partial.summary: The team escapes, but loses time and much of the best material.

failure.summary: The disturbance wipes out the working window and the party retreats with nothing fit to turn in.

nodes.label: Grade and deliver
nodes.summary: Sort the lot, discard the ruined scraps, and present the final bundle for payment.

checks.notes: Recognizing what is actually saleable.
Useful when the lot includes reagents or delicate botanicals.

success.summary: The client receives a clean lot and pays according to grade.

partial.summary: Enough survives the sorting table to satisfy the contract at reduced value.

records.name: Caravan Escort Contract
records.summary: A route-protection template for wagons, travelers, pilgrims, and similar escorted movement where ambushes, axle trouble, and formation discipline matter.

notes: Escort jobs need explicit route, formation, and casualty semantics in runtime; this archetype already exposes those branch points.
A larger group helps against open attack, but can make stealth, speed, and mountain travel worse.

classification.usualFailureProfile: Failure often means stolen cargo, injured clients, missed deadlines, or outright deaths when an ambush is not broken.

roleSlots.label: Route Lead
roleSlots.notes: Keeps the escorted party on the safest workable line.

roleSlots.label: Shield Guard
roleSlots.notes: Soaks first contact and holds the protected target together.

roleSlots.label: Rear Watch
roleSlots.notes: Catches pursuit, flankers, and high-ground raiders.

partySizeRules.effect: A thin escort risks instant collapse if an axle breaks at the same moment an attack begins.
Extra guards improve survival in a fight but slow the line, raise visibility, and can crowd narrow switchbacks.

outcomeMetrics.label: Client Safety
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the escorted party reaches the destination alive and intact.

outcomeMetrics.label: Cargo Integrity
outcomeMetrics.description: How much cargo, baggage, or draft stock survives undamaged.

outcomeMetrics.label: Route Speed
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the escort arrives before the hard deadline or shift window closes.

outcomeMetrics.label: Combat Control
outcomeMetrics.description: How cleanly the escort reacts when the route branches into a fight.

failureStates.label: Protected Target Lost
failureStates.description: A critical ambush or monster strike kills or captures the person being escorted.

failureStates.label: Cargo Scattered
failureStates.description: The team reaches the end with too little cargo left to satisfy the contract.

failureStates.label: Missed Window
failureStates.description: The escort arrives too late to satisfy the business, smelter, court, or convoy schedule.

nodes.label: Brief the route
nodes.summary: Choose the pace, order, and fallback points before the convoy rolls out.

checks.notes: Reading threat lines and bad terrain.
Without current route notes the escort starts blind.
More than one guard is expected on serious routes.
Some routes stay unsafe even with a good plan.

criticalSuccess.summary: The escort leaves with a disciplined march order and hidden fallback line.

success.summary: The team understands the route and expected contact points.

failure.summary: A weak route read sends the convoy straight into a dangerous bottleneck.

nodes.label: Hold the column
nodes.summary: Keep escorts, clients, wagons, and draft beasts moving in the order the route requires.

checks.notes: Protective spacing, shield control, and impact absorption.
March endurance and shield-line stamina.
Important if an axle or yoke starts to go.
A direct heal keeps the escort functional through a hard collision.
Weather and draft-beast behavior still matter.

criticalSuccess.summary: The convoy outruns trouble and arrives under tight control.

success.summary: The column stays together through the dangerous stretch.

partial.summary: A draft animal balks or a wheel slips, forcing the escort to defend under stress.

failure.summary: The line breaks and hostile eyes move in immediately.

nodes.label: Break the ambush
nodes.summary: Bandits, raiders, or beasts hit the weakest point of the route and must be contained fast.

checks.notes: Disciplined melee control matters when the escort starts to buckle.
Pulls threat off the escorted target at the key moment.
Helps the line survive the first collision.
A layered ward buys time if the escort is under-strength.
Useful when the escort needs to slow pursuit rather than win a clean kill.
Some attacks are simply heavier than expected.

criticalSuccess.summary: The escort crushes the contact before cargo or clients are meaningfully exposed.

success.summary: The attack is contained and the route can continue.

partial.summary: The escort survives, but loses cargo, time, or a draft animal in the scramble.

failure.summary: The line collapses and the protected target is lost or the convoy is scattered beyond recovery.

criticalFailure.summary: A catastrophic ambush breaks the escort completely and likely kills members of the convoy.

nodes.label: Handoff and account
nodes.summary: Deliver the living clients and surviving cargo, then argue over losses, lateness, or extra protection provided.

checks.notes: Good reporting can salvage pay after a rough route.

success.summary: The client signs off and pays according to survival, speed, and losses.

records.name: Extermination Sweep Contract
records.summary: A reusable threat-clearing template for vermin, lair monsters, raiders, or undead where the job is not done until the nest or source is confirmed neutralized.

notes: Extermination is not just combat: identification, breach choice, and proof of clearance all shift payout and failure risk.
Too few people may survive the kill but fail to fully clear eggs, brood, or hidden survivors.

classification.usualFailureProfile: The target may escape, multiply, or kill a party member if the breach goes wrong or the lair is misread.

roleSlots.label: Tracker
roleSlots.notes: Finds the real threat source instead of a decoy trail.

roleSlots.label: Breaker
roleSlots.notes: Commits to the breach and deals decisive damage.

roleSlots.label: Finisher
roleSlots.notes: Stops escape, brood survival, or undead recurrence.

partySizeRules.effect: Small teams can kill the visible target but often miss secondary nests, runners, or lingering corruption.
Larger parties reduce wipe risk but can trigger tunnels, stampedes, or alert behavior in cramped sites.

outcomeMetrics.label: Threat Removed
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the source of the infestation or hostile force is actually neutralized.

outcomeMetrics.label: Collateral
outcomeMetrics.description: How much infrastructure, stock, or habitat is damaged during the sweep.

outcomeMetrics.label: Proof of Kill
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the crew returns with credible confirmation rather than a guess.

outcomeMetrics.label: Survival
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the party clears the contract without deaths or crippling wounds.

failureStates.label: False Clearance
failureStates.description: The crew kills what it sees, but the nest or source remains active.

failureStates.label: Party Loss
failureStates.description: The breach costs a deployed character their life or combat viability.

failureStates.label: Target Escapes
failureStates.description: The core threat survives and relocates, often worsening later contracts.

nodes.label: Trace the source
nodes.summary: Find the true nest, brood room, den, shrine, or raider hold instead of the first visible symptom.

checks.notes: Separating the actual threat source from surface signs.
Improves spoor and nest-reading.
Useful if a scout or brood runner needs to be neutralized quietly.
Storms, smoke, or panicked victims can muddy the trail.

criticalSuccess.summary: The crew finds the core source and a favorable approach lane.

success.summary: The likely source is identified and the strike begins.

failure.summary: The crew enters on a bad angle and risks decoys, traps, or runners.

nodes.label: Force the breach
nodes.summary: Break into the nest or kill zone and survive the first violent exchange.

checks.notes: Axe force helps when a breach must be forced through barricade or bone.
Balanced reach and decisive finishing pressure matter once the room opens.
Helps secure the first kill at the cost of safety.
A stable defensive ward improves survival during the initial crash.
Unexpected numbers, trap density, or corruption can spike the danger.

criticalSuccess.summary: The breach lands perfectly and the target cluster breaks before it can scatter.

success.summary: The breach holds and the threat is on the back foot.

partial.summary: The party wins the room, but eats damage or lets a runner slip deeper.

failure.summary: The breach collapses and the threat tears through the party before a clean kill is secured.

nodes.label: Confirm the kill
nodes.summary: Make sure the contract target is actually dead, dormant, or cleansed instead of merely wounded or scattered.

checks.notes: Reading signs of survival, brood, or reanimation.
Fire and cleansing heat are especially useful against undead or corruption-heavy sites.
Burning eggs, resin, or residue can prevent a false clearance.
A second or third pair of hands helps sweep side chambers.
Some contracts hide a second chamber or delayed manifestation.

criticalSuccess.summary: The party wipes out the source and secures excellent proof.

success.summary: The threat is convincingly removed.

partial.summary: The visible target is gone, but signs suggest stragglers or collateral damage remain.

failure.summary: The crew leaves too early and the threat survives or reforms.

nodes.label: Report clearance
nodes.summary: Turn in proof, explain collateral, and let the issuer judge whether the place is actually safe again.

checks.notes: Useful when the job was ugly but still effective.

success.summary: The issuer accepts the clearance and issues payout based on proof and damage.

records.name: Porter and Delivery Run
records.summary: A logistics template for short-haul and medium-haul porter work where load balance, endurance, route handling, and final cargo condition decide pay.

notes: Porter work is not combat-first; most failures come from damage, lateness, route exhaustion, or dropping the wrong load order.
Instantiated contracts should specialize the route mode to foot, wagon, ferry, or mixed corridor.

classification.usualFailureProfile: A porter quest usually degrades into reduced reward for lateness or damaged freight, though route attacks and falls can still kill a carrier.

roleSlots.label: Lead Carrier
roleSlots.notes: Sets the pace and takes the burden of the critical load.

roleSlots.label: Route Runner
roleSlots.notes: Scouts bottlenecks and keeps the team moving when the route compresses.

roleSlots.label: Load Keeper
roleSlots.notes: Rebalances freight and prevents breakage.

partySizeRules.effect: A solo porter can finish light contracts, but heavy or awkward freight amplifies fatigue and damage risk.
Extra carriers help on bulk freight but can jam narrow roads, docks, or stairs and slow the overall route.

outcomeMetrics.label: Cargo Condition
outcomeMetrics.description: How intact, clean, and complete the delivered goods remain.

outcomeMetrics.label: Delivery Speed
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the load arrives inside the promised window.

outcomeMetrics.label: Carrier Fatigue
outcomeMetrics.description: How badly the team accumulates exhaustion or strain.

outcomeMetrics.label: Route Efficiency
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the team avoids costly detours, bottlenecks, and reload events.

failureStates.label: Late Delivery
failureStates.description: The cargo arrives after the relevant market, furnace, ferry, or civic window closes.

failureStates.label: Damaged Load
failureStates.description: The carried goods break, spill, or spoil before handoff.

failureStates.label: Carrier Break
failureStates.description: A fall, collapse, or attack takes the porter off the route entirely.

nodes.label: Balance the load
nodes.summary: Choose pack order, tie-down points, and who carries what before the route begins.

checks.notes: Knowing what a body or beast can actually carry.
Tie-down precision and stable packing.
Baseline hauling gear.
Transforms some freight runs entirely.
Some loads are inherently miserable.

criticalSuccess.summary: The load rides cleanly and fatigue starts low.

success.summary: The team gets the freight into workable balance.

failure.summary: A bad pack order guarantees trouble at the first narrow stretch.

nodes.label: Make the distance
nodes.summary: Carry, roll, or drag the freight through the main route without burning the team out.

checks.notes: Sustained load bearing and route endurance.
Maintaining pace without repeated drops.
Useful on stairs, docks, steep banks, or rubble where footing decides the pace.
Direct healing offsets the slow attrition that breaks long hauls.
A direct stamina buffer during deadline pushes.
Mud, traffic, ferries, and weather all slow the run.

criticalSuccess.summary: The team keeps pace and protects the load better than expected.

success.summary: The cargo makes the main route in good enough shape.

partial.summary: Fatigue, traffic, or shifting freight forces a stop mid-route.

failure.summary: A major stall or spill stops the run in a bad place.

nodes.label: Clear the bottleneck
nodes.summary: A blocked gate, steep ford, broken wheel, or hostile contact forces an emergency adjustment.

checks.notes: Useful for axles, crate braces, and broken drag poles.
A defensive stance helps a runner keep cargo moving when the route pinches shut.
Important if the bottleneck turns violent.
Some chokepoints eat time no matter what.

success.summary: The delay is contained and the freight survives.

partial.summary: The team gets moving again, but arrives late or with damaged stock.

failure.summary: The route break destroys the delivery window or the carried goods beyond acceptable recovery.

nodes.label: Inspect the delivery
nodes.summary: The receiver checks seals, counts packages, and judges whether the run was worth the quoted rate.

checks.notes: Useful when arguing over small losses or delays.

success.summary: The receiver accepts the run and pays based on condition and speed.

records.name: Standard Blacksmithing Commission
records.summary: A forge-work template for routine commissioned weapons, fittings, and tools using the natural smithing checkpoints of heating, forming, quenching, sharpening, and final adornment.

notes: This template is intentionally stage-driven so each natural forge step can improve or ruin the order.
Runtime still needs batch and partial-material accounting to fully realize catastrophic loss and reduced-yield branches.

classification.usualFailureProfile: Most failures lose material, quality, or delivery time, but burns and explosive cracks can also injure the smith.

roleSlots.label: Firekeeper
roleSlots.notes: Controls heat quality and timing.

roleSlots.label: Striker
roleSlots.notes: Adds force and consistency during shaping.

roleSlots.label: Finisher
roleSlots.notes: Handles the clean edge, fit, and any decorative finish.

partySizeRules.effect: Solo smithing is viable but creates tighter heat windows and more fatigue during long shaping phases.
Too many hands around one hearth create congestion and timing errors instead of better output.

outcomeMetrics.label: Forge Integrity
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the material survives each stage without cracking or warping beyond use.

outcomeMetrics.label: Final Quality
outcomeMetrics.description: How sharp, true, and attractive the finished piece is.

outcomeMetrics.label: Material Efficiency
outcomeMetrics.description: How much stock is lost to scale, splits, or total failure.

outcomeMetrics.label: Delivery Readiness
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the item is ready on time and fit for the client order.

failureStates.label: Catastrophic Crack
failureStates.description: A bad heat or quench destroys the entire workpiece.

failureStates.label: Warped Piece
failureStates.description: The order survives but falls to a lower quality tier or smaller final size.

failureStates.label: Forge Injury
failureStates.description: A flare, slip, or steam burst injures the crafter and can end the commission early.

nodes.label: Charge and heat
nodes.summary: Bring the stock to the correct working temperature without burning it or starting too cold.

checks.notes: Primary heat control.
Reading heat color and timing.
Helps keep the hearth even.
Useful when the hearth needs steady magical heat input.
Some fuel burns hotter or dirtier than expected.

criticalSuccess.summary: The metal hits the perfect working window and stays obedient on the anvil.

success.summary: The stock is hot enough for clean shaping.

partial.summary: The stock can still be worked, but scale and uneven heat eat into the margin.

failure.summary: The piece overheats or starts cold enough to crack under the first real shaping blow.

nodes.label: Form the profile
nodes.summary: Draw out the length, establish the shoulders, and shape the working body of the piece.

checks.notes: Core profile shaping skill.
Controlling hammer force and draw.
Keeping the line true during repeated strikes.
Baseline striking tool.
Fatigue and rebound can still twist the profile.

criticalSuccess.summary: The profile comes off the anvil straight, even, and ready for a clean heat treat.

success.summary: The item reaches an acceptable working shape.

partial.summary: The piece stays viable, but loses symmetry or mass in correction work.

failure.summary: A bad series of strikes folds or tears the workpiece beyond salvage.

nodes.label: Quench and temper
nodes.summary: Lock in the hardness without shocking the piece into a lethal crack or soft collapse.

checks.notes: Heat-treat judgment is where many commissions die.
Timing the drop and recovery.
Represents the prepared quench setup.
The hardest stage to fully control.

criticalSuccess.summary: The heat treat lands perfectly and gives the finisher an ideal base.

success.summary: The workpiece survives with acceptable hardness and alignment.

partial.summary: The piece survives but with a soft spot, warp, or brittle patch.

failure.summary: The quench destroys the piece in a total crack or twist.

nodes.label: Sharpen and fit
nodes.summary: Grind the edge or working face, correct balance, and fit the usable geometry.

checks.notes: Fine control during grinding and fitting.
A proper stone improves finish quality.
Even a good blank can chip under rushed finishing.

criticalSuccess.summary: The finish comes out sharp, balanced, and clean enough to impress.

success.summary: The item is fit for the commission and ready for any final trim.

partial.summary: The piece functions, but the edge or face shows mediocre workmanship.

failure.summary: A bad grind or fit ruins the commission beyond the agreed tolerances.

nodes.label: Adorn and inspect
nodes.summary: Apply any decorative finish, final polish, or order mark, then present the piece for acceptance.

checks.notes: Optional decoration or trim raises final value.
Presentation can help on borderline results.

success.summary: The client accepts the finished piece and pays by quality tier.

records.name: Damascus Blade Masterwork Commission
records.summary: A higher-order smithing template for layered blades where every fold-stack-weld pass is its own checkpoint before heat treatment, grinding, and final proofing.

notes: This archetype exists specifically to support multi-pass masterwork crafting rather than a single flat smithing roll.
Each fold-stack pass is intentionally separate so runtime can model cumulative fatigue, flaw carryover, and total-loss branches.

classification.usualFailureProfile: The most common failure is cumulative flaw build-up ending in a final crack, unusable pattern, or edge failure after many expensive stages.

roleSlots.label: Master Smith
roleSlots.notes: Owns the weld integrity and line of the blade.

roleSlots.label: Striker
roleSlots.notes: Adds force and speed during fold and draw phases.

roleSlots.label: Bench Finisher
roleSlots.notes: Handles polish, proof, and final presentation.

partySizeRules.effect: Solo execution is possible but greatly narrows the safe timing window across repeated fold passes.
Extra bodies around a masterwork hearth mostly add coordination errors instead of better throughput.

outcomeMetrics.label: Layer Integrity
outcomeMetrics.description: How well each fold and weld preserves the layered structure.

outcomeMetrics.label: Pattern Quality
outcomeMetrics.description: How attractive and coherent the final visible layering becomes.

outcomeMetrics.label: Edge Performance
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the blade survives proofing with the intended balance and bite.

outcomeMetrics.label: Material Loss
outcomeMetrics.description: How much expensive stock is wasted across the many passes.

failureStates.label: Weld Shear
failureStates.description: A fold-stack pass fails and the billet opens up under the hammer.

failureStates.label: Pattern Ruin
failureStates.description: The blade survives but loses the layered character required by the commission.

failureStates.label: Proof Break
failureStates.description: The blade fails at the final proof despite surviving all previous stages.

nodes.label: Prepare the billet
nodes.summary: Set the starting stock and heat so the first cut-and-stack pass begins on sound material.

checks.notes: Baseline masterwork threshold.
Reading the stock before the expensive passes begin.
Required for precise and safe handling.
Helps stabilize the first masterwork heat window.
Hidden flaws can start here.

criticalSuccess.summary: The billet begins with excellent heat and composition.

success.summary: The billet is ready for the first fold.

failure.summary: The starting billet is compromised before the true work even begins.

nodes.label: Fold, stack, and weld I
nodes.summary: Make the first cut-and-stack pass and draw the billet back out without opening the weld.

checks.notes: The first weld establishes the whole line.
Keeping the stack aligned during the weld.
Proper draw without flattening the stack badly.
Even a strong smith can lose a billet here.

criticalSuccess.summary: The first fold closes perfectly and leaves strong pattern potential.

success.summary: The billet holds and remains worthy of the second pass.

partial.summary: The billet survives, but an inclusion or slight drift enters the pattern.

failure.summary: The first weld shears and the stock is ruined.

nodes.label: Fold, stack, and weld II
nodes.summary: Repeat the fold on a now more expensive billet while preserving alignment and carbon balance.

checks.notes: The second pass compounds all earlier mistakes.
Maintaining the internal balance of the billet.
Useful on the longer, more exacting stages.
Small flaws widen here.

criticalSuccess.summary: The second fold tightens the line and improves final pattern clarity.

success.summary: The billet remains alive for the final fold.

partial.summary: The billet survives with creeping asymmetry or contamination.

failure.summary: The second pass opens the weld and wastes the commission stock.

nodes.label: Fold, stack, and weld III
nodes.summary: The final cut-and-stack pass decides whether the blade earns its masterwork status or dies under accumulated flaws.

checks.notes: Highest core smithing threshold in the archetype.
Any drift now will show forever.
Direct healing matters over long masterwork sessions that punish the body.
This is the make-or-break pass.

criticalSuccess.summary: The final fold lands with exceptional pattern potential and a healthy billet.

success.summary: The billet survives and can move to heat treatment.

partial.summary: The blade stock survives, but only a lower-grade pattern is likely now.

failure.summary: The billet tears or delaminates on the last fold, ending the commission.

nodes.label: Quench and temper the spine
nodes.summary: Heat treat the expensive billet into a blade without losing the line you fought to build.

checks.notes: Masterwork heat-treat threshold.
Represents the prepared quench bath and control.
The most expensive crack in the whole chain lives here.

criticalSuccess.summary: The blade takes an exceptional temper and carries its pattern cleanly.

success.summary: The blade survives the quench and remains proof-worthy.

partial.summary: The blade survives, but with a warp or softness that will show in proofing.

failure.summary: The masterwork cracks in the quench after all prior labor.

nodes.label: Prove and present
nodes.summary: Grind, polish, proof, and show the blade to the client as an actual commission rather than an unfinished bar of metal.

checks.notes: Optional hilt or decorative finish work.
Final polish, edge, and balance adjustments.
Improves edge proof quality.
The blade must still survive final proof.

criticalSuccess.summary: The blade proves cleanly and exceeds the prestige tier expected by the commission.

success.summary: The blade proves true and the client accepts the masterwork.

partial.summary: The blade survives as a respectable but not elite piece.

failure.summary: The blade fails proofing at the end of the entire chain.

records.name: Menial Labor Shift Contract
records.summary: A work-shift template for hauling sacks, dredging ditches, turning fields, clearing rubble, and similar low-prestige but essential labor jobs.

notes: Menial labor should still branch on pace, fatigue, congestion, and hazard response rather than collapsing into a single STR check.
The final instantiated job should decide whether the stage tools are hoes, shovels, rakes, handcarts, or sacks.

classification.usualFailureProfile: The usual failure is reduced output, spoilage, or avoidable injury rather than a dramatic wipe.

roleSlots.label: Labor Lead
roleSlots.notes: Keeps the shift moving and prevents the line from dissolving into waste.

roleSlots.label: Work Hands
roleSlots.notes: Carry the actual volume of work.

roleSlots.label: Hazard Runner
roleSlots.notes: Spots small collapses, vermin bursts, or unsafe footing before they cascade.

partySizeRules.effect: Small crews can finish light shifts but lose badly on bulk movement or cleanup volume.
Too many workers in one lane create congestion, wasted motion, and tool-sharing delays.

outcomeMetrics.label: Output Volume
outcomeMetrics.description: How much actual work the crew completes during the shift.

outcomeMetrics.label: Waste
outcomeMetrics.description: How much grain, stone, soil, or work time is wasted through bad handling.

outcomeMetrics.label: Fatigue
outcomeMetrics.description: How badly the shift drains the deployed party.

outcomeMetrics.label: Safety
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the crew avoids the avoidable injuries and small hazards common to labor work.

failureStates.label: Shift Shortfall
failureStates.description: The crew ends the window with too little work done to satisfy the contract.

failureStates.label: Avoidable Injury
failureStates.description: The shift loses a worker to strain, collapse, or mishandled tools.

failureStates.label: Spoilage or Scatter
failureStates.description: Poor handling wastes too much of the moved or processed material.

nodes.label: Take the assignment
nodes.summary: Pick rows, lanes, piles, or wagons so the crew does not waste the shift before the first lift.

checks.notes: Choosing the right work order.
Directing workers cleanly matters on bigger crews.
The crew size needs to match the volume.
Some sites start in worse shape than expected.

criticalSuccess.summary: The crew starts on the cleanest, highest-yield section and wastes almost no time.

success.summary: The shift begins with a workable division of labor.

failure.summary: Bad lane choice or clutter forces a slow correction early in the shift.

criticalSuccess.summary: The crew keeps rhythm and outperforms the expected volume.

success.summary: The shift meets the expected labor target.

partial.summary: Fatigue or tool delays force a messy middle-shift correction.

checks.notes: Spotting the real cause instead of thrashing around it.
Direct healing keeps the crew from losing a worker to strain.

records.name: Maritime Salvage Charter
records.summary: A waterborne recovery template for wrecked cargo, lost nets, broken skiffs, and drifted loads where currents, rigging, and timing decide the result.

notes: Maritime salvage in the current foundation leans on extraction skill for rigging, recovery, and physical water work rather than a dedicated traversal skill.
More crew can help haul a wreck free, but can also overload a small recovery craft.

classification.usualFailureProfile: Failure typically means lost cargo, damaged recovery gear, or drowning risk when the water turns faster than expected.

roleSlots.label: Pilot
roleSlots.notes: Keeps the salvage craft on the right line.

roleSlots.label: Diver
roleSlots.notes: Cuts lines, checks the snag, and secures the real recovery point.

roleSlots.label: Rigging Hand
roleSlots.notes: Handles the pull, balance, and cargo transfer.

partySizeRules.effect: A tiny crew may find the wreck but fail to secure or haul it before the current turns.
Too many bodies on a small salvage platform or skiff can make the recovery itself unsafe.

outcomeMetrics.label: Cargo Recovered
outcomeMetrics.description: How much of the target load or wreck is actually brought back.

outcomeMetrics.label: Water Safety
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the crew survives the current, rigging strain, and exposure.

outcomeMetrics.label: Hull Damage
outcomeMetrics.description: How much wear the recovery craft suffers during the job.

outcomeMetrics.label: Timing
outcomeMetrics.description: Whether the recovery happens before the tide, current, or weather fully shifts.

failureStates.label: Lost to Current
failureStates.description: The target cargo or wreck slips away before the recovery secures it.

failureStates.label: Crew Overboard
failureStates.description: The salvage turns into a rescue and the original contract effectively fails.

failureStates.label: Recovery Craft Broken
failureStates.description: The job damages the boat or rig so badly the crew cannot finish.

nodes.label: Mark the drift
nodes.summary: Read current, wind, and floating signs to find where the real target will be when the crew reaches it.

checks.notes: Route knowledge and reading the water decide the cleanest salvage line.
Reading water and wind.

Water does not respect the plan.

criticalSuccess.summary: The crew reaches the target on the cleanest possible line.

success.summary: The target line is found and the rigging phase can begin.

failure.summary: The salvage craft arrives late and the crew must improvise directly on the snag.

nodes.label: Rig the recovery
nodes.summary: Get the lines, hooks, and pull points set before current or surf tears the target loose again.

checks.notes: Core salvage rigging.

Pulling and holding the line under strain.
Hardware and current can still fight the crew.

criticalSuccess.summary: The rig catches cleanly and the haul starts under control.

success.summary: The target is secured and ready to come home.

partial.summary: The rig holds only partly and the divers must finish the job in the water.

failure.summary: The first rigging attempt fails and the water gets more dangerous by the minute.

nodes.label: Dive or cut free
nodes.summary: A diver goes in to free a snag, secure the real anchor point, or save the line before current wins.

checks.notes: Freeing a snag and securing the real recovery point is extraction work under pressure.
Staying useful under cold, panic, and drag.
A defensive ward offers a small safety edge against debris and glancing impacts.
Direct healing matters when salvage turns into emergency recovery.
Some snags are simply bad luck waiting to happen.

success.summary: The diver frees the target and the crew can still salvage most of it.

partial.summary: The target comes free, but the crew loses time, cargo, or a clean recovery line.

failure.summary: The water wins and the crew loses the target or nearly loses a diver with it.

nodes.label: Haul and claim
